newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Emboldened opposition to march in Belgrade again.
newsitem.headline: Emboldened opposition to march in Belgrade again.

text.p: Anti-government protestors will rally in Belgrade on Wednesday, defying Serbian President Slobodan Milosevic, after a day of violent clashes in the city.
Rival groups of pro and anti-Milosevic demonstrators fought running battles with wooden clubs and iron bars, as the two camps converged on the city centre for mass rallies on Tuesday.
One man was shot in the head by a supporter of the ruling Socialist Party (SPS) and badly injured.
It was the first violence after more than a month of street protests by students and the Zajedno (Together) opposition coalition against alleged election fraud by ruling Socialists.
Thousands were expected to protest in the capital on Wednesday, fired by their success in facing down a rally organised by Milosevic to intimidate them.
The autocratic ruler ferried in some 40,000 backers from outside the capital, a much lower figure than expected.
Western states condemned Milosevic's decision to stage his rally at the same time and place as the regular Zajedno rallies.
Acting U.S. Secretary of State Strobe Talbott said the move was largely responsible for the violence.
France also blamed Milosevic for provoking the clashes, while Germany expressed grave concern at the lack of dialogue between the two sides.

Most of the violence was before and after the rival gatherings. Some 40,000 SPS supporters listened to Milosevic, while more than 200,000 people followed Zajedno's leaders on a march through the surrounding city streets.
Milosevic, making his first public appearance since the crisis over disputed local election results began in mid-November, told supporters no one would be allowed to destabilise Serbia.
"A strong Serbia is not to the liking of many powers outside our country," he said. "That is why, together with the fifth column they have formed here, they have tried to destabilize our country."
Diplomats said the relatively small turnout for Milosevic would encourage opposition supporters to join what is widely expected to be a record march on Wednesday.

"Milosevic has scored an own-goal," said one Western diplomat who declined to be named. "He only had one chance at his demonstration and he blew it. Now all his people have gone home and I don't think they'll come back in a hurry."
"I reckon this will only give the Zajedno supporters the shot of adrenalin they need to get back on the streets."
State television's evening national news bulletin only showed pictures of the pro-Milosevic demonstration as the participants drove home on board hundreds of comandeered buses.
Many said they had been given the day off work in state-run factories and ordered to come to Belgrade, and were completely unaware of the opposition protests.
"Who are they?" inquired one elderly SPS supporter when she saw a group of students marching through the city. "I had no idea there was anybody unhappy with our president."

Zajedno leader Zoran Djindjic told supporters: "Milosevic has clearly turned full circle and has gone back to provoking disturbances. Belgrade was quiet until he brought his supporters here. The minute they came, the shooting began."
